enquiry: We run a cell culture process in an aqueous medium. Glucose and lactate are measured from samples, and the delay makes it difficult to see changes promptly. We are exploring an in situ spectroscopy pilot that can be checked against those existing laboratory measurements. The medium and cell population change during the run; we have not yet selected a probe or a calibration strategy.

intake.summary: A cell culture process in aqueous medium wants to move glucose and lactate measurement from delayed sample-based laboratory analysis towards an in situ spectroscopy pilot, with the existing laboratory measurements used as the comparison. The medium and cell population change during the run, and no probe or calibration strategy has been chosen.

recommendations.rationale: Mid-IR is described as highly informative with well-defined bands, and an ATR probe gives the very thin sample layer that strong mid-IR water absorption requires. It is a defensible alternative single method to compare against Raman.
recommendations.conditions: Applies where the probe keeps tight contact with the liquid and crystal fouling can be managed.

citations.quote: Vibrational spectroscopy in the mid-IR range (4000-400 cm-1) is one of the most informative methods of chemical analysis.

recommendations.rationale: Mid-IR and Raman spectra are complementary, and a combined ATR plus Raman fiber probe has been shown, so a fused model is a plausible later hypothesis. It is only worth the second instrument if it beats the best single method on held-out runs.
recommendations.conditions: Only if neither single method covers both analytes across the changing medium and cell population.

solution_options.cost_drivers: two spectrometers, combined probe, synchronisation and fused-model work
solution_options.fusion_note: Start with one model per method as the baseline, then fuse the synchronised Raman and mid-IR blocks, scaled so that neither method dominates the joined model. The two probes must look at the same measurement point, and the two data streams must be normalised to a common time step before fusion, with each method keeping its own calibration and diagnostics. Keep the fused model only if it beats the best single method on held-out runs or batches.

citations.quote: The analysis of such systems may require a combination of two or even more spectral methods.
This property makes mid-IR and Raman spectra complementary, that is, they complement each other.
It is crucial that the spectral information obtained by different methods-Mid-IR, NIR, Raman, and fluorescence spectra-is collected from the same small, even pinpoint, area of the sample.
Ultimately, the measurement data must be normalized to a common time step.

proposal.what_would_change_it: Answers on the glucose and lactate range, the required accuracy and the medium's optical density could change the choice: a strongly scattering, high-cell-density medium would favour MIR-ATR or the combined option, while a clear, low-scattering medium would bring NIR transmission or reflection back into the shortlist. A strong fluorescence background on real samples would move the choice away from Raman.
proposal.next_step: Run the first feasibility experiment on representative process samples and compare the in-situ predictions with the existing laboratory glucose and lactate values.

assessment.brief_answer: Test Raman first as a single in-situ method: it suits an aqueous medium and is reported to give a molecular fingerprint for glucose and lactate. A mid-IR ATR probe is the natural single-method comparison. Still open: the concentration range and required accuracy, the medium's optical behaviour, the probe location, and what counts as agreement with the laboratory values. A combined Raman + ATR model is a later hypothesis only.
